findings.detail: The `build-sign` job runs arbitrary branch code: the checked-out composite action, `scripts/check-release-version.sh`, `provider-signing-validation.py` and `Package.swift`. Its outputs (`version`, `source_sha`, `binary_hash`, `bundle_hash`, `metallib_hash`, `code_directory_hash`) are passed unvalidated into the `publish` job's env. `publish` holds `DEV_RELEASE_KEY` and the dev R2 keys. The workflow does not re-check that `VERSION` matches `X.Y.Z-dev.branch.N`, recompute the hashes from the downloaded bundle, or confirm that `RELEASE_SOURCE_SHA` is the commit that was built. A malicious branch can therefore emit a forged version, a master SHA as source provenance, or hashes that differ from the bundle. The master `prepare` script may reject some of these, but that is not visible here. The result is a blessed-hash registration (A-011) on the dev coordinator with spoofed provenance, and a version string that can steer the installer's relaxed ad-hoc signature path. Fix: in `publish`, validate the version with a strict regex, recompute every hash from the downloaded tarball, and derive the source SHA from the trusted run context (not from job output) before any credentialed step.
findings.title: Publish job trusts identity values emitted by the untrusted branch-build job

findings.detail: The header says the file is dispatched on master and that the credentialed `publish` logic is the reviewed master copy. Nothing enforces this. `workflow_dispatch` executes the workflow definition from whichever ref is selected. A collaborator with write access can dispatch a branch whose copy of this file has an altered `publish` job. That job can read `DEV_RELEASE_KEY`, the dev R2 keys and the dev coordinator URL, because they are repo-level secrets with no protected environment. The master-checkout of the scripts does not prevent this. The result is theft or abuse of the dev release credentials (A-005), and registration of arbitrary binary hashes in the dev blessed-hash registry (A-011). Fix: add `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/master'` on both jobs, or use a protected environment with required reviewers, and restrict branch-ref dispatch.
findings.title: Credentialed dev-publish workflow has no guard that it runs from the reviewed master definition

findings.detail: `pip install awscli` is unpinned and unhashed. The tool then runs in steps that hold `DEV_R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `DEV_R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `DEV_RELEASE_KEY`. A compromised or typosquatted package release would execute with those secrets. Fix: pin the version with hashes, or use a preinstalled or checksum-verified CLI.
findings.title: Unpinned awscli installed immediately before steps that hold R2 and release credentials

findings.detail: The new docs describe `select_provider_identity` and `verify_staged_app_signature` relaxing the designated requirement to only the bundle identifier `io.darkbloom.provider` whenever the version string contains `-dev.` or `-staging.`. The only code-identity check left is the identifier, so any ad-hoc binary with that identifier passes. The selector is a substring of the version returned by the release API. The safety argument relies on 'a prod coordinator is never served a pre-release version', which is an unverified deployment assumption. A mis-registered, compromised or poisoned release response carrying a `-dev.` marker would downgrade the installer to unsigned-code acceptance on a production machine. The dev and prod installs also share the bundle identifier, APNs topic and the root fan helper `io.darkbloom.fan-helper`. This weakens the code-identity assumptions behind T-013, T-034, T-054 and T-044, and the threat model does not describe the new self-signed tier. Fix: gate the relaxed requirement on the installer's dev coordinator binding (the host it was fetched from), not on the returned version string. Refuse the marker when the prod coordinator is bound. Confirm the fan helper and MDM/APNs paths still require the Developer ID team requirement. Add the self-signed tier to TB-009, TB-011 and T-054.
findings.title: Installer drops Apple-anchor/team check for any `-dev.`/`-staging.` version, accepting arbitrary ad-hoc code

findings.detail: The new `release-dev-branch.yml` lane lets any workflow-dispatch writer publish a build of any `ref` to the dev coordinator with `DEV_RELEASE_KEY`, without merge or review. The docs state that, because `/v1/releases/latest` orders by `created_at`, the branch build becomes the latest dev release and a fresh install takes it. The dev coordinator 'hashes the bundle rather than inspecting the Apple signature', so registration of a self-signed build does not imply the Developer ID identity assumed in T-054 and A-017. Provider operators on dev could be served unreviewed code that handles consumer plaintext (A-001). Mitigations to document or enforce: restrict dispatchers, require a protected environment or approval for `DEV_RELEASE_KEY`, avoid `latest` aliasing for branch builds (use an opt-in channel), and record in the threat model that dev-tier providers must never receive production-sensitive traffic.
findings.title: Dispatch of arbitrary branch publishes unreviewed code as dev `latest` for fresh installs

findings.detail: select_provider_identity now picks DARKBLOOM_PRERELEASE_DESIGNATED_REQUIREMENT (`identifier "io.darkbloom.provider"` only) whenever the version contains `-dev.` or `-staging.`. That version comes from the same /v1/releases/latest response that supplies the URL and hashes. The only guard is a comment saying a prod coordinator is never served a pre-release version. The installer does not enforce this, even though PRODUCTION_COORD_URL is defined in the same file. A compromised or misconfigured release feed, or a prod install pointed at a non-prod coordinator, can return a `-dev.` version. The installer then accepts any ad-hoc signed bundle claiming that identifier, with no Developer ID or team-OU check. This removes the Developer ID check that backs the bundle-hash and URL checks. It also weakens the binary-integrity assumptions in T-013, T-034 and A-011 for an installer that holds provider keys and decrypted prompts. The new dev-branch lane makes self-signed builds from arbitrary branches routinely publishable, which raises the exposure. Fix: apply the relaxed requirement only when the effective coordinator is explicitly a non-production host (not PRODUCTION_COORD_URL). Alternatively, make it a build-time property of the dev installer snapshot that the prod installer cannot reach.
findings.title: Installer drops the Apple-anchor signature pin based on an API-supplied version string

findings.detail: select_provider_identity now chooses the relaxed requirement `identifier "io.darkbloom.provider"` whenever VERSION contains `-dev.` or `-staging.`. VERSION is parsed from the same /v1/releases/latest response that supplies url, bundle_hash, binary_hash and metallib_hash. The installer never checks that COORD_URL is a dev or staging coordinator, and it does not compare it with PRODUCTION_COORD_URL. The comment 'a prod coordinator is never served a pre-release version' is a server-side assumption, not an installer check. Previously the Apple-anchor/team-OU pin on the staged app was the independent control. It held even if the release record, bundle URL, bundle hash or binary hash were attacker-controlled. Now anyone who can alter or poison the release record can bypass it. Examples are a compromised release-registration key (A-005), a bad registry entry, or a hostile coordinator for a non-production COORD_URL. The attacker sets version to something like `9.9.9-dev.1` or `9.9.9-staging.1` and ships a self-signed or ad-hoc bundle that carries the right bundle identifier and a matching hash. The installer accepts it and runs `runtime-smoke` from it. The install is then committed and the app handles consumer plaintext and the provider keys. Fix: apply the relaxed requirement only when COORD_URL is an explicitly allow-listed non-production host. Production-built installers should keep the full Apple-team requirement unconditionally. Alternatively, gate the relaxation behind an explicit opt-in flag or environment variable that is not derived from server-supplied data.
findings.title: Installer drops the Apple Developer ID anchor based on an untrusted version string from the release JSON

findings.detail: The new `-staging.` marker relaxes the signature requirement. However, identity selection still maps only `-dev.` to the separate `darkbloom-dev` identity and path. A `-staging.` version falls into the default branch: CLI_NAME=darkbloom, APP_NAME=Darkbloom.app and INSTALL_DIR=~/.darkbloom. A self-signed or ad-hoc staging build therefore replaces the production app via commit_staged_app. It also repoints the /usr/local/bin and PATH symlinks and writes the staging coordinator into the production provider.toml. This breaks the stated isolation property at lines 42-45 for staging. It also means one weakened-signature artifact installs directly into the production identity and keychain access-group context. Fix: give staging its own identity and paths, or refuse relaxed-signature installs that would target the production identity.
findings.title: Staging pre-release builds share the production identity and install path, so a relaxed-signature build overwrites the production install
